analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices, taxes sudden price spikes, and allows importing cheaper drugs from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in any of its three committees and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill took aim at prescription drug prices on several fronts at once. It directed Medicare to negotiate prices with drug makers, imposed an excise tax of up to 100% of the revenue from price increases above medical inflation, required drug companies to disclose their costs, profits, and executive pay, allowed Americans to import safe lower-priced drugs from Canada, capped out-of-pocket drug costs at $250 a month, and closed loopholes that keep cheaper generics off the market. It never moved past committee referral in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who pay some of the highest drug prices in the developed world because federal law barred Medicare from negotiating; people with high drug cost-sharing under employer plans and ACA plans; and patients facing sudden price increases, who would get the transparency of public reporting and, on the industry side, a stiff tax on spikes. Low-income seniors would gain a new manufacturer rebate that brings Medicare drug pricing closer to Medicaid levels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and patients with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the law (the 'non-interference' clause) that prohibits Medicare from negotiating Part D drug prices, requiring the Secretary to negotiate prices for high-spending drugs and, if negotiation fails after a year, to set the price at the lower of the VA's procurement price [S3].

It imposes an excise tax on price spikes: 50% of the excess revenue for increases above medical inflation, 75% for 15-20% increases, and 100% for increases of 20% or more, with the proceeds funding NIH research [S3].
It caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month ($500 per family) in qualified health plans and group health plans starting in 2019 [S3].

It requires manufacturers to report annually on R&D spending, marketing and advertising, gross and net profits, executive compensation, and federal benefits received, with civil penalties up to $200,000 per day for noncompliance, all published publicly [S3].

It directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to permit importation of qualifying prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers, including 90-day personal-use supplies, and bans manufacturers from discriminating against or cutting off supply to such sellers [S3].

It requires drug makers to pay Medicare rebates, roughly matching Medicaid rebate levels, for drugs dispensed to low-income Part D beneficiaries, and accelerates closing the Part D coverage gap from 2020 to 2018 [S3].

It targets tactics that keep generics off the market, including product hopping and anticompetitive patent-settlement deals the FTC could challenge, and disallows the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer prescription drug advertising [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the direct costs: Medicare-negotiated prices, an excise tax on price-spike revenue, expanded rebate obligations, mandatory public disclosure of costs, profits, and executive pay, and new competition from imported drugs and generics. Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers face new reporting duties on rebates and prices. Some drug makers argue the transparency and pricing provisions would reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Secretary broad discretion to 'negotiate' prices with a fallback of setting them at VA procurement levels if talks fail, which critics warned could function as de facto price-setting and, industry argues, reduce incentives and revenue for developing new drugs [S3].

The excise tax on price spikes is a blunt instrument: a legitimate increase driven by higher manufacturing costs is exempted only if the Inspector General verifies it, and the tax applies to cumulative increases over five years, which drug makers argued could penalize normal price growth on older low-cost drugs [S3].

Importation shifts safety oversight to a new certification regime for foreign pharmacies and sellers; the bill itself acknowledges the risk with counterfeit-drug suspension authorities and new criminal penalties for fraudulent online pharmacies [S3].

The bill is sprawling, touching Medicare negotiation, tax policy, antitrust, FDA regulation, and import law across three committees, which made its path through Congress difficult even for sympathetic members [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of Americans on Medicare and insured patients with high drug cost-sharing, the potential savings were large and came at the expense of a single concentrated industry's profits, not ordinary taxpayers or consumers. The honest trade-off is the industry's argument that cutting U.S. drug revenue means less drug R&D, and the real risk that price controls of this design could slow some drug development. The transparency, generic-competition, and importation provisions carried little of that risk while directly lowering prices, making the package's benefits hard to dismiss; its problem was never design ambition but that it never reached a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat with three House committees after introduction, was referred to health subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 29, 2017, joined by Reps. Elijah Cummings, Rosa DeLauro, and Peter Welch as original cosponsors [S1].

The Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — and it was subsequently sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where its record ends [S5].
The bill's action history after the subcommittee referrals shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].
All 23 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and Republicans held the House majority and all three committee chairmanships during the 115th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they avoided Medicare price negotiation, the price-spike excise tax, importation competition, and mandatory profit disclosure. Medicare beneficiaries and patients with high drug costs gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill died in committees controlled by House Republicans, who held the majority and every committee chairmanship involved.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions — Medicare price negotiation with a VA-price fallback, an excise tax of up to 100% of price-spike revenue, Medicaid-level rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees, public disclosure of costs, profits, and executive pay, and bans on supply cutoffs to Canadian sellers — directly transfer revenue and pricing power from manufacturers to Medicare beneficiaries and patients. Its failure left current pricing law untouched.

The bill would have required public reporting of net drug prices after PBM rebates, exposing how rebate dollars flow between manufacturers and PBMs, and reducing the opacity PBMs have relied on. PBM transparency became law years later through other means.

Importation provisions would have created a certified-seller program letting Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers legally serve American patients, winning them a new customer base while lowering patients' costs.
The bill narrowed the 180-day generic exclusivity period and targeted product hopping and pay-for-delay settlements, expanding generic competition and lowering prices for consumers.
